blocks.text: דוב (Bechoroth 8a) and דובא (B. mez. 85b*). The Talmud compares the Persians to the bear in the following four respects. Like it, they eat much, are heavily covered with flesh, very hairy and restless (Kiduschin 72a). Here Raschi explains that the bear, bound to a chain, walks back and forth. Raschi explains more simply on A. Sara 2, 6: the bear is wont to walk constantly back and forth, which is why it is called דובא ניידא "restless bear" (Kiduschin ibid.). These four qualities do indeed belong to the bear. It is voracious, so that it swallows its food almost without chewing, and its voracity has become proverbial. Its fatness helps it to pass the winter almost without nourishment. Its fur is woolly and thick-haired, becoming somewhat smoother only with age. Finally, it is wont to be in constant motion, as can be observed when it is in an enclosure. It stays near the forest so that it can flee quickly when danger approaches (Sota 47a). It is considered more dangerous than the lion, although it is inferior to it in strength (Sanhedrin 98b), which the Tosephot (A. Sara 2b. s.v. ואריא) explain by saying that the bear is more inventive. Probably what is meant here are its keenly developed senses, which, except for sight, are extraordinarily sharp in the bear.

Because of its dangerousness, trade in it is forbidden (A. Sara 16a); yet it is tamable (B. Kama 15b), which is especially the case when it is caught young. Into old captured bears one inserts an iron ring through the nose, to which a chain is fastened, which Raschi had in mind in his explanation mentioned at the beginning.**) Its gestation lasts three years (Bechoroth 8a, and on this §. 17).

אנקה (already biblical, related by transposition to Ἐχῖνος [Echinos]; Raschi: הריצון, Hérisson, Chulin 122a), קפור, or קפור ((Bartenoro: ארצו, Spanish Erizo, Kilajim 8, 5) and יילי (B. batra 4a, which Sachs erroneously takes for Ἴουλος [Ioulos], see on this in detail §. 446). Bartenoro on the cited passage says: "קפור is an animal whose body is entirely covered with spines and which, when touched, draws in its feet and rolls itself up like a ball."
This happens because the skin of the back is developed on the inside into a powerful muscle, with which the animal can enclose its head, belly and paws and so make itself unassailable.

Raschi (B. batra ibid.) says: שערו קשה כמחטין "Its hair hard as needles", more precisely the same on Sabbat 54b: נימין חדים כמחט "Its spines sharp (i.e., pointed) as needles"; for the hedgehog has no guard hairs, but spines.

One used to tie the hedgehog skin (which in itself is soft, Chulin 122a) around the udders of cows so that the יאלי would not suck the milk from them (Sabbat 54b). The Talmudic word יאלי is explained in various ways. Raschi translates it as leeches, against which the Tosephot already rightly remark that leeches are never called יאלי and in any case suck only blood, not milk; they therefore take it in the sense of יילי, by which, as mentioned at the beginning, the hedgehog is designated. This explanation, however, is no happier, for firstly it is unknown that the hedgehog sucks milk, and then קפור rather than יאלי should have been used, since the former word is mentioned immediately before.

Maimuni (Sabbat 5, 4) takes the word for snakes, which are wont to suck the milk from sleeping cows, but which are scared away by the rattling of the hedgehog spines. Snakes do indeed love milk (§. 105) and have keen hearing, so that they are scared away by the slightest noise (§. 33); but snakes are no more called יאלי than leeches are, which is why I may be permitted to add a conjecture. The Hebrew radix יאל has the meaning "to begin, to commence" and could thus serve as a designation for a "young one", which began its existence a short while before. One therefore tied a hedgehog skin around the udders of the cows in order to prevent the calves from sucking, and the word would be read יְאֳלִי; [p. 101] the Jerusalem Talmud (Sabbat 7, c) explains that practice entirely in the sense suggested.

With the hedgehog skin the eyes of a martyr were put out (B. batra 4a). In the passage B. Kama 80a, where it says that one raises cats, fox-spitzes, large weasels and קופין for catching mice, Bochart (Hieroz. P. I. lib. 3, cap. 36, col. 1036) more correctly reads קופרים "hedgehogs" for קיפין, since apes are by no means trained to catch mice (see the articles Ape and Spider). The hedgehog, as is well known, thoroughly exterminates mice and cockroaches.

On the other hand, Bochart wrongly translates in the Talmudic passage (Berachoth 57b): "The elephant and the קפוד are in a dream apparitions announcing misfortune", by "hedgehog", since here the word means guenon (see this article), as reference is being made here to the partial resemblance of the animal to man.

חנשמת (Chulin 63a), באוח (ibid. *), קרפראי (Berachoth 57b), קורפראי (Raschi: טלפא, Talpa, Chulin 63a) and אישות (Kelim 21, 3). The Jerusalem Talmud takes אשה (see Tos. on Moed Katan 6b. s.v. צרין) for חולדה "weasel", which misleads Bochart into translating the biblical חולד as "mole" (Hieroz. P. I, lib. 3, cap. 35, col. 1024); but it is beyond doubt that the Babylonian Talmud does not understand אישות as weasel, since Kelim 21, 3 speaks of the catching of the אישוה "moles" and ibid. 15, 6 of the catching of the חולדה "weasel", so that the two names absolutely cannot be identical. The view of the Jerusalem Talmud can perhaps be explained by the fact that both animals share several qualities and were considered related genera. Both animals are carnivorous, burrow under the earth, are short-footed, short-tailed and have a delicate, soft pelt.
